pages.text:
*Garden Log, Day 8: Growing: pea (4.5 cm). Patience (0.1 cm).*

Seven days is a long time for a pea. I counted the seconds. I measured the light. I watered it at dawn, before the sun hit the concrete, and again at dusk, when the sky turned the color of a bruised plum. Gherkin watched me with eyes that did not blink. He pointed a claw at a rusted watering can sitting in the corner.

"Always been there," he said. "Use it."

The can was bent in the middle, like a tired knee. The handle was smooth from years of hands. I filled it from the tap behind the loading bay. The water tasted like metal and rain. I poured it slowly, watching the soil darken. Then I took out my tape measure.

Four and a half centimeters. That is not much. But it is a lot for a pea. I opened the notebook Mama bought me for schoolwork. The cover said *English*. I crossed out the word with a black pen and wrote *Garden Log*. My handwriting was messy. I did not care. It was the first thing I had made that was mine.
pages.image: Sana, in an oversized denim jacket, pours water from a rusted, bent watering can onto a small green pea sprout in a walled garden; an old tortoise with a mossy shell watches from the side, and morning light filters through leaves.

pages.text:
School was louder than Yusuf’s fire alarm. I sat in the back row near the window, watching dust motes swirl in the sunbeams. I never put my hand up, not because I didn’t know the answers, but because I didn’t want to say them out loud where everyone could hear.

Theo Kowalski slid into the seat next to me, a skateboard tucked under his arm. He wore a beanie and a hoodie with the sleeves pushed up. He looked at me, then at the clock, then at me again.

"You look like you have been up at dawn," he said. "Doing crime."

I did not look at him. "Gardening."

He laughed. It was a short, sharp sound, then he laughed again, harder. He had to sit down on his skateboard to stop himself from falling over, and the board screeched against the linoleum floor like a dying cat.

I hated him. I counted the seconds. One, two, three. Nine. He was still laughing. I turned back to my window. The dust motes were dancing still.
pages.image: A boy in a beanie and hoodie sits on a skateboard in a classroom, laughing hard with his head thrown back; a girl with round glasses and a low black bun sits beside him, looking away with a flat, unimpressed expression.

pages.text:
I wanted the pea to grow faster, so I decided to help it along with some science that was only half-scientific. I took a spoonful of Yusuf’s crushed cornflakes and poured them onto the soil, then dragged an extension lead across the concrete and plugged in a desk lamp. I stood there and sang, not because I had a song, but because I felt like I was supposed to.

The pea did nothing. So I planted a tomato seed and told it a true thing, which was "I am tired of waiting."

It grew. It grew so fast that the air around it seemed to buzz with effort. In one hour, it had seventeen tomatoes, red and heavy and shiny, and the stem bent under their weight until the whole plant groaned and fell over. It lay on the ground, a heap of red fruit and green leaves, looking thoroughly exhausted.

Gherkin blinked slowly. "Mm," he said. "Show-off."
pages.image: A tomato plant lies collapsed on the garden ground, weighed down by a cluster of bright red tomatoes; a thin girl in a denim jacket stands over it with a pout, while a mossy tortoise looks on with indifference.

pages.text:
The tomato was a disaster, mostly red and mostly broken. I picked up the pieces, feeling the guilt settle into my chest like heavy wet sand. Then I took out the tin and read the rules again, my finger tracing the words: one seed a day, one true thing. I chose a new seed, small and brown, and held it in my palm until it warmed up.

"I get scared when people look at me," I said.

My voice was tiny and wobbly, shaking like a phone signal with one bar left, but I did not stop. I planted it.

Three days later, a flower appeared. It was blue and tiny, shaped exactly like a school bell. I whispered to it, asking it to be quiet.

It rang.

It was a faint sound, a single sharp note that cut through the air. It was the best thing I had ever grown, not made, but grown, and it was mine.
pages.image: A tiny, delicate blue bell flower stands in a small patch of soil; a thin girl with brown skin and round glasses leans in close, her lips parted in a whisper, her expression soft and surprised.

pages.text:
I read the tin again, turning it over in my hands until the metal felt warm. The scratches on the bottom were deep, much deeper than I had noticed before, and the letters were smaller than the rest.

*Someone must speak for it when the day comes.*

I looked at Gherkin, who was chewing a piece of lettuce with the speed of a glacier. "What day?" I asked.

"Mm," he said, and then, much later, "Not yet."

The air in the garden went still, and the blue flower stopped its faint ringing. My neck went cold, a feeling like I had just realized I forgot my homework. I did not know what day he meant, or what I would have to say, but I knew I would have to say it. I took out my tape measure and held it against the stem. Two centimeters. I wrote the number down in my notebook, closed the cover, and walked to the gap in the fence.
pages.image: A thin girl with a green pencil in her hair holds a small tape measure near a tiny blue flower; an old tortoise with a mossy shell sits nearby, its expression unreadable, in a quiet, sunlit garden corner.
